questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a board evaluate how a presenter recovers from a mistake as a separate skill from the mistake itself?
options: Because mistakes are automatically disqualifying regardless of recovery
Because boards never notice mistakes in the first place
Because a calm, clean correction often costs less credibility than the original mistake, while a mistake left to compound or badly covered up costs far more than the mistake itself would have
Because recovery skill and the underlying mistake are always scored identically
questions.explain: Mistakes under live pressure are normal and expected. What's separately evaluated is the recovery -- a clean correction tends to cost less credibility than the original error, while a poorly handled or hidden mistake costs much more.

questions.q: Which recovery does this lesson recommend specifically for a design inconsistency, such as contradicting an earlier statement about your own design?
options: Acknowledge the contradiction exists but leave both versions unresolved for the board to sort out
Actually resolve the contradiction by stating which version is correct and briefly why, rather than just noting the conflict exists
Ignore the contradiction entirely and hope it isn't noticed
Restart the entire presentation from the beginning
questions.explain: A design inconsistency needs actual resolution -- stating which version is correct and briefly why -- so the board isn't left holding two conflicting claims about the same design.

questions.q: What does this lesson's recommended correction pattern specifically avoid doing?
options: Stating the accurate version of the correction
Naming that a correction is being made at all
Continuing the presentation after making the correction
An extended apology and re-litigating in detail how the mistake happened, which draws more attention to the error and eats time for no real benefit
questions.explain: The pattern is short: name the correction, state the accurate version, continue -- without an extended apology or re-explaining the full context of how the error happened, which only draws more attention to it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say hoping an inconsistency goes unnoticed is almost always the wrong bet with an experienced panel?
options: Because panels are legally required to ignore all inconsistencies
Because reviewers are listening carefully as part of the job, and a reviewer catching the inconsistency later in Q&A reads worse than if the presenter had caught and fixed it themselves
Because panels never ask follow-up questions that could reveal an inconsistency
Because self-correction is always seen as a sign of weakness
questions.explain: An experienced panel is listening carefully, and being caught in an inconsistency you could have fixed yourself reads worse than catching it yourself -- self-correction signals you're tracking your own presentation, while being caught signals the opposite.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect self-caught mistakes to the CTA review board's expectations described in Lesson 5?
options: The CTA board only rewards revisions a judge catches, never ones the candidate catches themselves
Self-caught mistakes are treated as automatic point deductions in the CTA format

Training material describes the board expecting candidates to adjust a solution live when they realize something doesn't hold up, not only when a judge points it out -- the self-caught version is simply the stronger showing of that same skill
The CTA board has no expectation at all around revising a solution mid-session
questions.explain: The same defend-and-revise judgment extends to self-caught issues -- the board's training material describes expecting candidates to adjust their solution live upon realizing something is wrong, and catching it yourself is the stronger demonstration of that same skill.
